Fix a finite integer $e \ge 2$ and charge $0$, with the independent-root affine
Cartan datum, its lattices and its diagram reflection $\tau$ fixed as in
[[def-cyclic-affine-type-a-cartan-datum]]: $I = \mathbb{Z}/e\mathbb{Z}$, simple
roots $\alpha_i$, fundamental weights $\Lambda_i$, $\delta$, and
$\tau(i) = -i$. A *node* is a pair $(r,c) \in \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$, and
the *residue* of a node is $\operatorname{res}(r,c) := c - r \bmod e$; this is
the level-one, charge-$0$ specialization of the residue used in
[[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]]. We use the
English convention (rows increase downwards) and the node language of
[[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]] and
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]].

A partition $\lambda$ is **$e$-regular** if every positive integer occurs as a
part of $\lambda$ fewer than $e$ times, and **$e$-restricted** if
$\lambda_a - \lambda_{a+1} < e$ for every $a \ge 1$, the sequence being padded
by trailing zeros; these are the prime-case notions of
[[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]] with $e$ in place of the prime
$p$. A column of height $e$ is allowed in an $e$-restricted partition. The two
classes are exchanged by conjugation: $\lambda$ is $e$-restricted if and only if
its conjugate $\lambda'$ is $e$-regular (step 2.1 below).

**The modular (restricted) signature.** Let $\lambda$ be a partition and
$i \in I$. The $i$-nodes of $\lambda$ are its addable and removable nodes of
residue $i$; list them *top to bottom*, that is by increasing row index and then
increasing column index, obtaining $A_1,\dots,A_n$, and form the word
$\sigma = (\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n)$ with $\sigma_m = +$ if $A_m$ is addable and
$\sigma_m = -$ if $A_m$ is removable. Whenever $r < s$ with $\sigma_r = -$,
$\sigma_s = +$ and $\sigma_{r+1} = \dots = \sigma_{s-1} = 0$, replace
$\sigma_r,\sigma_s$ by $0$; repeat until no $-$ lies above a $+$. The survivors
are the *normal* removable and *conormal* addable $i$-nodes; write
$\varepsilon_i(\lambda)$ and $\varphi_i(\lambda)$ for their numbers. If
$\varepsilon_i(\lambda) > 0$, the *good* $i$-node is the removable node
belonging to the first surviving $-$, and $\tilde e_i\lambda := \lambda$ with
that node deleted; if $\varphi_i(\lambda) > 0$, the *cogood* $i$-node is the
addable node belonging to the last surviving $+$, and $\tilde f_i\lambda$ is
$\lambda$ with that node added (otherwise the respective partial operator is
undefined). This is Kleshchev's reduced $i$-signature at charge $0$ and level
one, with good $=$ top normal and cogood $=$ bottom conormal. **This is the
reading used for the restricted (symmetric-group) model**, in which the labels
of the level-one basic module are the $e$-restricted shapes; Fayers' equivalent
formulation reads the same list with the opposite cancellation and extracts the
last surviving $- $ and first surviving $+$, and his increasing-column model of
the $e$-restricted labels is the basic crystal $B(\Lambda_0)$.

**The linear (symmetric-group) model and the transport $J$.** Let
$$F_{\mathrm{QG}} = \bigoplus_{\lambda} \mathbb{Q}(q)\,|\lambda\rangle$$
be the charge-$0$ level-one partition Fock space with
$\operatorname{wt}(|\lambda\rangle) = \Lambda_0 - \sum_i m_i(\lambda)\alpha_i$,
where $m_i(\lambda)$ is the number of nodes of $[\lambda]$ of residue $i$, and
with the declared finite node operators $F_i$, $E_i$, $K_h$, $K_d$ and the wedge
bar $\psi$ of [[def-level-one-partition-fock-space-and-node-residues]] (the
operators act on *all* partitions). The **symmetric-group model** $F_{\mathrm{sym}}$
is the same $\mathbb{Q}(q)$-vector space with the basis relabelled
$M_\lambda := |\lambda'\rangle$; equivalently, $J : F_{\mathrm{sym}} \to F_{\mathrm{QG}}$
is the $\mathbb{Q}(q)$-linear isomorphism
$$J M_\lambda = |\lambda'\rangle \qquad (\lambda \text{ a partition}),$$
with the field map $q \mapsto q$ (not $q \mapsto q^{-1}$). Transport the
structure along $J$:
$$E_i^{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} E_{-i}^{\mathrm{QG}} J, \qquad F_i^{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} F_{-i}^{\mathrm{QG}} J, \qquad K_h^{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} K_{\tau h}^{\mathrm{QG}} J \quad (h \in P^\vee), \qquad \psi_{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1} \psi J,$$
and give $M_\lambda$ the weight
$\operatorname{wt}(M_\lambda) := \Lambda_0 - \sum_i m_i(\lambda)\alpha_i$. The
transported operators are defined on the ambient basis of *all* partitions.
With $A := \mathbb{Z}[q,q^{-1}]$ and the local ring
$A_0 := \{\, f \in \mathbb{Q}(q) : f \text{ is regular at } q = 0 \,\}$, the
**standard chart** of the symmetric-group model is
$$(F_0)_{\mathrm{sym}} := \bigoplus_{\lambda} A_0\, M_\lambda ;$$
the full ambient model is indexed by all partitions, while its basic component
in this convention is carried by the $e$-restricted shapes (the comparison with
the QG model is made by the results of this page).

**Label dictionaries and boundaries.** The conjugation map $C : \lambda \mapsto \lambda'$
exchanges the $e$-restricted and the $e$-regular partitions, preserves the
addable/removable *type* of each node and negates residues; it is a comparison
map *between* the restricted and the regular models, not an involution of one
label set, and it is not the same-model sign (Mullineux) involution of
Kleshchev's Theorem 11.8, which fixes the restricted label set and negates
residues along a good-node path. In the symmetric-group regime (ground field of
characteristic $p > 0$, Hecke parameter $\xi = 1$, so that $e = p$ is prime) the
$e$-restricted partitions are the labels of the simple modules in the
dual-Specht convention and the $e$-regular partitions those of James, the two
dictionaries being related by
$D(\lambda) \cong D^{\lambda'} \otimes \operatorname{sgn}$, equivalently
$D^\mu \cong D(\mu') \otimes \operatorname{sgn}$ for $e$-regular $\mu$
([[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]]);
for a general Hecke parameter the finite integer $e \ge 2$ is its quantum
characteristic (the smallest positive $e$ with $1 + \xi + \dots + \xi^{e-1} = 0$)
and need not be prime, so the general finite-$e$ crystal labels are not called
symmetric-group modules of "characteristic $e$". At quantum characteristic
$e = 0$ (no such positive integer exists, colors $\mathbb{Z}$) no finite affine
datum is present: every level-one partition is a crystal label, and no weight
formula or finite affine statement is made in this boundary.

Let $F:=\bigoplus_{\lambda}\mathbb Q(q)|\lambda\rangle$ be the charge-$0$ part of
the Fock space of
[[lem-semi-infinite-wedges-are-indexed-by-partitions-and-give-node-action-formulas]],
with basis indexed by all partitions and with the node operators $F_i,E_i$
defined by the stable finite-prefix action. Assign to $|\lambda\rangle$ the
**level-one weight**

$$\mathrm{wt}(|\lambda\rangle):=\Lambda_0-\sum_{i\in I}m_i(\lambda)\,\alpha_i, \qquad m_i(\lambda):=\#\{\text{cells of }\lambda\text{ of residue }i\},$$

where the **residue** of a cell in row $r$ and column $c$ is $c-r\bmod e$, and
the **size** $|\lambda|$ is the separate grading. The vacuum is the empty
partition $\varnothing$; $F_i$ adds and $E_i$ removes a node by the explicit
finite node formulas of the same item. The toral action is
$K_i|\lambda\rangle=q^{N_i(\lambda)}|\lambda\rangle$ with $N_i$ the
addable-minus-removable count, proved to be the Cartan pairing in
[[lem-the-node-count-is-the-level-one-cartan-pairing]], and
$K_d|\lambda\rangle=q^{-m_0(\lambda)}|\lambda\rangle$.

A partition is **$e$-regular** if each positive part occurs with multiplicity
$<e$, and **$e$-restricted** if $\lambda_r-\lambda_{r+1}<e$ for every $r\ge1$
(with $\lambda_{r}=0$ beyond the length). These operators are declared linear
endomorphisms here; the affine relations proved later establish the actual
module structure, so nothing about $F$ is silently assumed in this Definition.

The constructed node operators on **all** partition vectors make the charge-$0$
partition Fock space $F$ into a $P$-graded integrable module for
$U_q(\widehat{\mathfrak{sl}}_e)$ with the fixed coproduct and the cyclic Cartan
datum: all toral commutation rules and mixed commutators
$[E_i,F_j]=\delta_{ij}(K_i-K_i^{-1})/(q-q^{-1})$ hold, and both quantum Serre
sums vanish, including the cubic $e=2$ case with
$a_{01}=a_{10}=-2$ and $[3]=q^2+1+q^{-2}$. Each color acts on finite Boolean
cubes, and $F_i,E_i$ change the $P$-weight by $\mp\alpha_i$. Ordinary standard
coefficients may have $q^{-1}$ poles; normalized Kashiwara lattice stability is
a separate statement.

Work in the linear symmetric-group model of
[[def-symmetric-group-level-one-residue-and-partition-label-convention]]: the
$\mathbb{Q}(q)$-linear isomorphism $J M_\mu = |\mu'\rangle$, the transported
action, bar and $A_0$ standard chart $(F_0)_{\mathrm{sym}}$, and the weight
$\operatorname{wt}(M_\mu) = \Lambda_0 - \sum_i m_i(\mu)\alpha_i$, with
$A = \mathbb{Z}[q,q^{-1}]$.

**The basic module and its lower basis.** Let
$M_{\mathrm{sym}} := J^{-1}V(\Lambda_0) = J^{-1}M_{\mathrm{QG}}$ be the
transported highest-weight module of the vacuum; by
[[thm-restricted-partition-component-is-the-basic-crystal-in-the-symmetric-group-convention]]
its crystal is the $e$-restricted component and its labels are the $e$-restricted
partitions. For an $e$-restricted $\lambda$ define
$$G_{\mathrm{sym}}(\lambda) := J^{-1}G_{\mathrm{QG}}(\lambda'),$$
where $G_{\mathrm{QG}}(\mu)$ is the lower global (canonical) basis element of
the Fock space at the standard vector $|\mu\rangle$
([[thm-the-basic-representation-global-basis-is-unitriangular-in-the-partition-basis]]).
Then $G_{\mathrm{sym}}(\lambda) \equiv M_\lambda \bmod q\,(F_0)_{\mathrm{sym}}$
and the family $\{G_{\mathrm{sym}}(\lambda)\}$ is the transported lower global
basis of $M_{\mathrm{sym}}$, indexed by the restricted labels. Define the
**level-one transition polynomials in the symmetric-group convention** by the
finite weightwise expansion
$$G_{\mathrm{sym}}(\lambda) = \sum_\mu d_{(\lambda,\mu)}(q)\, M_\mu ,$$
the sum being over the partitions $\mu$ of the weight of $\lambda$.

**Ambient polarization and ambient upper coordinates.** Define the ambient
polarization by $B(M_\mu,M_\nu) = \delta_{\mu\nu}$ on the standard basis, a
symmetric nondegenerate bilinear form on each finite weight space. Fix a weight
$w$ and let $V_w$ be the (finite-dimensional) weight space of
$F_{\mathrm{sym}}$; let $D_{\mathrm{rect}}$ be the matrix with columns the
coordinate vectors of $G_{\mathrm{sym}}(\lambda)$ for the finitely many
$e$-restricted $\lambda$ of weight $w$, and rows the **standard** shapes
$M_\mu$, $\mu$ of weight $w$; let
$$H := D_{\mathrm{rect}}^{\mathsf{t}}\, D_{\mathrm{rect}} , \qquad G_{\mathrm{sym}}^*(\lambda) := \sum_\mu \bigl(D_{\mathrm{rect}}H^{-1}\bigr)_{(\mu,\lambda)}\, M_\mu^* ,$$
where $M_\mu^*$ denotes the ambient orthonormal dual frame of the standard
basis. The $G_{\mathrm{sym}}^*(\lambda)$ are the **ambient upper coordinates**
of the basic module: they are the unique elements of the basic subspace
$(M_{\mathrm{sym}})_w\subseteq V_w$ characterized weightwise by $B(G_{\mathrm{sym}}^*(\lambda), G_{\mathrm{sym}}(\lambda')) = \delta_{\lambda\lambda'}$,
and are viewed in the ambient standard frame; adding a vector of the
$B$-orthogonal complement in $V_w$ gives other ambient representatives with
the same pairings. The coefficients
$e_{(\lambda,\mu)}(q) := (D_{\mathrm{rect}}H^{-1})_{(\mu,\lambda)}$ lie in
$\mathbb{Q}(q)$ but need not be Laurent integral or polynomial. They are
coordinates in the ambient space and not a "standard basis of the basic
module"; the exact integral upper basis is the transported upper global basis of
[[thm-upper-and-lower-global-bases-are-dual-and-crystal-compatible]], whose
restricted graded $A$-dual lattice is free weightwise and perfectly paired with
the basic lower $A$-span, while no lower-$A$ selfduality, no $A$-unit $H$ and no
full algebraic duality in infinite rank is implied. The restriction of $B$ to the basic module equals the normalized transported
contravariant form (proved in step 4.2), so these are the same upper vectors
viewed in the ambient standard frame and in their own integral dual lattice.
Upper bar is the adjoint bar
$\psi^\vee$ with its own dual infinity chart and weighted upper operators, not
the ordinary lower bar.

**The full ambient case.** On the whole Fock space the analogous matrix
$D_{\mathrm{full}}$, with columns the $G(\mu)$ over all partitions and rows the
standard shapes, is unitriangular (diagonal $1$, in $q\mathbb{Z}[q]$ below the
diagonal), and the dual matrix with respect to $B$ is
$$D_{\mathrm{full}}^{-\mathsf{t}},$$
which is Laurent integral because the inverse of a unitriangular matrix with
entries in $\mathbb{Z}[q]$ has entries in $\mathbb{Z}[q]$.

**A worked instance.** At $e = 2$ the restricted shape $\lambda = (1,1)$ has
$G_{\mathrm{sym}}(1,1) = M_{1,1} + q\,M_{2}$, so $D_{\mathrm{rect}}$ has the
single column $(q,1)^{\mathsf{t}}$, $H = 1 + q^2$, and
$$G_{\mathrm{sym}}^*(1,1) = \frac{M_{1,1}^* + q\,M_2^*}{1+q^2} = \frac{M_{1,1} + q\,M_2}{1+q^2},$$
an explicit ambient coordinate that is rational but not Laurent integral:
$1 + q^2$ is not a unit of $\mathbb{Z}[q,q^{-1}]$. No specialization of the $d$

Let $F$ be a field and $q\in F^{\times}$ an invertible element. The **quantum
characteristic** $e=e(F,q)$ is the least integer $e\ge2$ such that
$1+q+\cdots+q^{e-1}=0$ in $F$, and $e:=\infty$ when no such integer exists
([[def-q-integer-q-factorial-and-q-multinomial]],
[[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Since $[1]_q=1\ne0$, the least positive
integer $e$ with $[e]_q=0$, when it exists, automatically satisfies $e\ge2$, so
the two formulations coincide.

Concretely: (i) if $q\ne1$ then $[m]_q=(q^m-1)/(q-1)$ for all $m\ge0$ — indeed
$(q-1)(1+q+\cdots+q^{m-1})=q^m-1$ and $q-1\ne0$ — so $[e]_q=0$ is equivalent
to $q^e=1$, and a finite $e$ exists exactly when $q$ is a root of unity and
then $e$ is the multiplicative order of $q$ in $F^{\times}$ (which is $\ge2$
because $q\ne1$); (ii) if $q=1$ then $[m]_1=m$, so $e=\operatorname{char}(F)$
when $\operatorname{char}(F)>0$ (the characteristic is a prime, hence at least
$2$, and $m\cdot1_F\ne0$ for $1\le m<p$) and $e=\infty$ when
$\operatorname{char}(F)=0$
([[prop-group-algebra-and-finite-field-specializations-of-the-generic-hecke-algebra]]).

If $e<\infty$ then $q\ne1$ implies $q^e=1$, and hence $[m+e]_q=[m]_q$ for
every integer $m$: for $m\ge0$ the sum splits as
$$[m+e]_q=[m]_q+q^m[e]_q,$$
so $[m+e]_q=[m]_q$ whenever $[e]_q=0$; for the remaining $m<0$ one extends the
closed formula by $[m]_q:=(q^m-1)/(q-1)$ when $q\ne1$ and reads $[m]_1:=m\in F$
for the canonical image of the integer $m$ when $q=1$, in which case
$e=\operatorname{char}(F)$ and $[m+e]_1=m+e=m$ in $F$. In particular the
quantum characteristic, not merely the multiplicative order, is the parameter
governing the modular representation theory of the Hecke algebra. No choice
principle is used.

Fix an integer $e\ge 2$ and put $I:=\mathbb Z/e\mathbb Z=\{0,1,\dots,e-1\}$
with its cyclic order; elements of $I$ are called **residues**. Let
$A=(a_{ij})_{i,j\in I}$ be the integer matrix with

$$a_{ii}=2,\qquad a_{i,i-1}=a_{i,i+1}=-1\ \ (i\in I)$$

$a_{01}=a_{10}=-2$ when $e=2$; all indices are read modulo $e$. Thus for

([[def-symmetrizable-cartan-datum-for-a-quantum-group]]).

with the $\mathbb Z$-bilinear pairing $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:P\times

$$\langle\Lambda_j,h_i\rangle=\delta_{ij},\qquad \langle\delta,h_i\rangle=0,\qquad \langle\Lambda_j,d\rangle=0,\qquad \langle\delta,d\rangle=1 .$$

Define the **simple roots**

$$\alpha_i:=\sum_{j\in I}a_{ji}\Lambda_j+\delta_{i0}\,\delta\qquad(i\in I),$$

let $Q:=\bigoplus_{i\in I}\mathbb Z\alpha_i\subseteq P$ be the **root lattice**
and $Q^+$ its nonnegative cone, and define the **central element**
$c:=\sum_{i\in I}h_i\in P^{\vee}$. The **level** of $\lambda\in P$ is

Let $\lambda\vdash n$ with Young diagram $[\lambda]$, and let
$\mu\vdash n-1$ and $\nu\vdash n+1$ denote partitions of the neighbouring
sizes ([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).

A node $x\in[\lambda]$ is **removable** if deleting it leaves a Young diagram,
that is, if there is a partition $\mu\vdash n-1$ with
$$[\mu]=[\lambda]\setminus\{x\};$$
such a $\mu$ is unique because a partition is determined by its diagram. A
point $y\notin[\lambda]$ is **addable** for $\lambda$ if inserting it leaves a
Young diagram, that is, if there is a partition $\nu\vdash n+1$ with
$$[\nu]=[\lambda]\cup\{y\};$$
again $\nu$ is unique. We write $\operatorname{Rem}(\lambda)$ and
$\operatorname{Add}(\lambda)$ for the sets of removable and of addable nodes
of $\lambda$.

Since $[\lambda]=\{(i,j):1\le i\le k,\ 1\le j\le\lambda_i\}$ is determined by
the inequalities $1\le j\le\lambda_i$, the two conditions have the following
row form. Write $\lambda_{k+1}:=0$ for a partition $\lambda=(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_k)$.
A node $(i,\lambda_i)$ is removable if and only if
$\lambda_i>\lambda_{i+1}$: deleting the last node of row $i$ keeps the row
lengths weakly decreasing exactly when row $i+1$ is strictly shorter, and no
node $(i,j)$ with $j<\lambda_i$ can be deleted, since the node
$(i,j+1)$ would then have no node to its left. Similarly a node
$(i,\lambda_i+1)$ with $1\le i\le k$ is addable if and only if $i=1$ or
$\lambda_{i-1}>\lambda_i$, the node $(k+1,1)$ opening a new row is always
addable, and these are all the addable nodes. In particular a row endpoint of
$[\lambda]$ is removable only if no node of $[\lambda]$ lies immediately
below it.

For the empty partition the diagram is empty, so
$\operatorname{Rem}(\varnothing)=\emptyset$, while
$\operatorname{Add}(\varnothing)=\{(1,1)\}$ is a single node, whose insertion
produces the partition $(1)$.

Work in the regime of
[[def-nondegenerate-root-of-unity-level-one-hecke-regime]]. Fix a partition
$\mu$, put $d=|\mu|$, $\alpha=\operatorname{cont}(\mu)$, and let $K(\mu)$ be
the $F$-span of the Murphy elements $m_{S,T}$ of
[[def-arbitrary-level-cyclotomic-hecke-murphy-cell-and-schur-modules]] with
$S,T$ standard tableaux of a multipartition strictly dominating $\mu$; by
`thm-arbitrary-level-cyclotomic-hecke-murphy-basis-is-cellular` $K(\mu)$ is a
two-sided ideal of $H^\Lambda_d$ and $z_\mu:=m_{t^\mu t^\mu}+K(\mu)$ is
defined. Define the (level-one) **cell/Specht module**
$$S(\mu):=H^\Lambda_d\,z_\mu\subseteq H^\Lambda_d/K(\mu),$$
a LEFT $H^\Lambda_d$-module lying in the block $H^\Lambda_\alpha$.

For every standard $\mu$-tableau $T$
([[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]) fix a reduced decomposition
$w_T=s_{r_1}\cdots s_{r_m}$ of the associated permutation and put
$z_T:=T_{w_T}z_\mu$, $v_T:=\psi_{w_T}z_\mu$ in the Khovanov--Lauda presentation
of `def-type-a-cyclotomic-specialization-of-the-qg-klr-algebras`. For a
removable $i$-node $A$ of a partition $\lambda$
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]]) define
$$d_A(\lambda):=\#\{\text{addable }i\text{-nodes strictly below }A\}-\#\{\text{removable }i\text{-nodes strictly below }A\}$$
(equivalently in the level-one symmetric residue convention of the regime) and
define the **degree** of a standard tableau inductively by
$\deg(\varnothing):=0$ and, for $d>0$,
$\deg(T):=\deg(T_{\le d-1})+d_A(\mu)$ where $A$ is the node of $T$ containing
$d$.

The definition asserts, and
`thm-graded-specht-module-has-homogeneous-tableau-basis` on this page proves,
that $\{v_T:T\in\operatorname{Std}(\mu)\}$ is a homogeneous $F$-basis of
$S(\mu)$ making it a graded $R^\Lambda_\alpha$-module whose $q$-character is
$\operatorname{ch}_qS(\mu)=\sum_Tq^{\deg T}i_T$; forgetting the grading
recovers the ungraded cell module. **Convention.** This is the LEFT Murphy cell
module, obtained from the right cellular datum by $h\cdot m=m h^*$. Forgetting
its grading, `thm-dj-bridge-murphy-cell-is-the-same-shape-specht-dual`
identifies it with the star-contragredient dual of the same-shape
independently defined ordinary Dipper--James Specht module $P(\mu)$. Separately,
`thm-dj-bridge-ordinary-specht-is-the-signed-conjugate-murphy-cell` gives
$S(\mu)\cong P(\mu')^{\theta}$ after the same left-module conversion. These are
two proved module comparisons, not the identification of an untwisted conjugate
module. The sign pullback may change ordinary residue content from $-\alpha$ to
$\alpha$; these ungraded comparisons do not assert homogeneity of the ordinary
form or of a raw Hecke sign automorphism in the fixed transported grading. The
labelling of simples by $e$-restricted or $e$-regular partitions is NOT asserted
here; it is determined by the head-classification theorem later on this page.

No choice is used in the definition.

Fix an integer $e\ge 2$ and put $I:=\mathbb Z/e\mathbb Z=\{0,1,\dots,e-1\}$
with its cyclic order; elements of $I$ are called **residues**. Let
$A=(a_{ij})_{i,j\in I}$ be the integer matrix with

$$a_{ii}=2,\qquad a_{i,i-1}=a_{i,i+1}=-1\ \ (i\in I)$$

when $e\ge 3$, and with $a_{00}=a_{11}=2$ and the single double edge
$a_{01}=a_{10}=-2$ when $e=2$; all indices are read modulo $e$. Thus for
$e\ge3$ all off-diagonal entries other than the neighbouring entries $-1$ are
$0$, and for $e=2$ the matrix is
$\begin{pmatrix}2&-2\\-2&2\end{pmatrix}$. Take the diagonal symmetrizer
$D=\operatorname{diag}(1,\dots,1)$ and the quantum parameter $q$ over
$\mathbb Q$, so that $q_i=q^{d_i}=q$ for every $i\in I$
([[def-symmetrizable-cartan-datum-for-a-quantum-group]]).

Choose free abelian groups

$$P=\Bigl(\bigoplus_{i\in I}\mathbb Z\Lambda_i\Bigr)\oplus\mathbb Z\delta, \qquad P^{\vee}=\Bigl(\bigoplus_{i\in I}\mathbb Z h_i\Bigr)\oplus\mathbb Z d,$$

with the $\mathbb Z$-bilinear pairing $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:P\times
P^{\vee}\to\mathbb Z$ determined by

$$\langle\Lambda_j,h_i\rangle=\delta_{ij},\qquad \langle\delta,h_i\rangle=0,\qquad \langle\Lambda_j,d\rangle=0,\qquad \langle\delta,d\rangle=1 .$$

Define the **simple roots**

$$\alpha_i:=\sum_{j\in I}a_{ji}\Lambda_j+\delta_{i0}\,\delta\qquad(i\in I),$$

let $Q:=\bigoplus_{i\in I}\mathbb Z\alpha_i\subseteq P$ be the **root lattice**
and $Q^+$ its nonnegative cone, and define the **central element**
$c:=\sum_{i\in I}h_i\in P^{\vee}$. The **level** of $\lambda\in P$ is
$\langle c,\lambda\rangle\in\mathbb Z$ ([[def-kac-moody-integral-and-dominant-integral-weights]]),
and the **classical weight lattice** is $P_{\mathrm{cl}}:=P/\mathbb Z\delta$.

The **diagram reflection** $\tau$ is the pair of $\mathbb Z$-linear
involutions $\tau:P\to P$, $P^{\vee}\to P^{\vee}$ with
$\tau(\Lambda_i)=\Lambda_{-i}$, $\tau(\delta)=\delta$, $\tau(h_i)=h_{-i}$ and
$\tau(d)=d$ (indices negated in $\mathbb Z/e\mathbb Z$).

The **normalized affine weight form** is the symmetric $\mathbb Q$-bilinear form on $P_{\mathbb Q}:=P\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb Q$ determined, in the decomposition $P_{\mathbb Q}=Q_{\mathbb Q}\oplus\mathbb Q\Lambda_0$, by

$$(\alpha_i,\alpha_j)=a_{ij},\qquad (\Lambda_0,\alpha_i)=\delta_{i0},\qquad (\Lambda_0,\Lambda_0)=0.$$

Thus, for $x=\sum_i x_i\alpha_i$, $y=\sum_i y_i\alpha_i$ and $t,s\in\mathbb Q$, set

$$(x+t\Lambda_0,y+s\Lambda_0)=\sum_{i,j}x_i a_{ij}y_j+t y_0+s x_0.$$

In particular $(\lambda,\alpha_i)=\langle\lambda,h_i\rangle$ and $(\lambda,\delta)=\langle\lambda,c\rangle$. Its restriction to $Q$ is integer-valued; on all of $P$ it is rational-valued. This form on weights is distinct from the weight-coweight pairing. Define $s_i(\lambda):=\lambda-\langle\lambda,h_i\rangle\alpha_i$ and let $W$ be the group generated by these simple reflections; the form is $W$-invariant and $\tau$-invariant.

For a realization as in [[def-realization-of-a-generalized-cartan-matrix]], set $Q=\bigoplus_{i=1}^n\mathbb Z\alpha_i$ and $Q^+=\bigoplus_{i=1}^n\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\alpha_i$. Define $\operatorname{ht}(\sum_i k_i\alpha_i)=\sum_i k_i$. For $\lambda,\mu\in\mathfrak h^*$ write $\mu\le\lambda$ if $\lambda-\mu\in Q^+$.

Independence of the simple roots makes coordinates unique. Thus $Q^+\cap(-Q^+)=\{0\}$, which proves antisymmetry of the order; closure under addition proves transitivity, and $0\in Q^+$ proves reflexivity. Positive roots will belong to $Q^+\setminus\{0\}$, not all of $Q^+$.

Retain English Young diagrams, an $l$-multicomposition $\mu$ of $d$, its
diagram, and the row-reading initial standard tableau $t^\mu$, in which
$1,2,\dots,d$ appear in order along the successive rows from top to bottom
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]); for a single
component this is the standard tableau of
[[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]. A $\mu$-tableau $T$ is a
placement of $1,\dots,d$ in the nodes of $\mu$. It is **row-strict** if its
entries increase from left to right in every row of every component, and
**standard** if it is row- and column-strict. The group $S_d$ acts on tableaux
by its action on entries, and for a $\mu$-tableau $T$ the permutation $w_T$ is
defined by $w_Tt^\mu=T$. The **strong Bruhat order** on tableaux is
$$S\le_BT\quad:\Longleftrightarrow\quad w_S\le w_T$$
in the Bruhat order of [[def-bruhat-order-on-the-symmetric-group]], identified
with its one-based realization as in
[[lem-bruhat-order-basic-properties-for-permutations]]. We write $S\unlhd T$
for $S\le_BT$ and $S\lhd T$ for strict order; the separately declared meaning
of $\unrhd$ on partitions ([[def-dominance-order-on-partitions]]) is not
reused for tableaux. On row-strict $S,T$ the order $\unlhd$ is equivalent to
the prefix-shape comparison
$$\operatorname{sh}(S^{\le a})\unrhd\operatorname{sh}(T^{\le a})\quad\text{for every }a,$$
where $T^{\le a}$ erases the nodes occupied by entries $>a$ and
$\operatorname{sh}$ records the resulting row lengths read in row-reading
order; this row-sequence dominance is distinct from the weak Bruhat order and
must not be reversed. The transposition criterion is
$$S=(a_1\,b_1)\cdots(a_m\,b_m)T$$
with $a_n<b_n$ and $b_n$ occupying an earlier row-reading node than $a_n$ in
$(a_{n+1}\,b_{n+1})\cdots(a_m\,b_m)T$ for each $n$.

For entries $r,s$ of one component define $r\to_Ts$ if they lie in the same row
and $s$ is strictly to the right of $r$; $r\downarrow_Ts$ if they lie in the
same column and $s$ is strictly below $r$; and $r\nearrow_Ts$ if $s$ is
strictly above and strictly right of $r$ (south-west is the reverse of
$\nearrow_T$). A **weak Bruhat graph edge** $T\xrightarrow{r}S$ requires both
tableaux standard, $S=s_rT$, and $r$ occupying an earlier row-reading node
than $r+1$. Equivalently $r+1\nearrow_Tr$, or $r$ lies in an earlier component
than $r+1$. In particular a same-row or same-column swap is NOT a standard
edge. A **terminal path** is a directed path in this graph, and $T$ is
$(r_1,\dots,r_m)$-**terminal** if there are standard tableaux
$S_1\xrightarrow{r_1}S_2\xrightarrow{r_2}\cdots\xrightarrow{r_m}T$.

The **Garnir belt** at a node $(a,b,n)$ with $(a+1,b,n)$ also a node of $\mu$
consists of the nodes $(a,c,n)$ for $b\le c\le\mu_a$ and the nodes
$(a+1,g,n)$ for $1\le g\le b$. The **Garnir tableau** of shape $\mu$ at
$(a,b,n)$ is the unique maximal standard $\mu$-tableau in the order $\unlhd$
among the standard $\mu$-tableaux agreeing with $t^\mu$ outside the
$(a,b,n)$-Garnir belt; it equals $t^\mu$ in the degenerate case
$b=1=\mu_a$. A **horizontal brick** is a string of consecutive entries along
same-row right arrows. The following source facts are retained with these
exact conventions and are proved below: the transposition criterion and the
prefix-shape criterion; the row-strictness of a vertical consecutive swap and
its exceptional-prefix comparison; agreement outside the Garnir belt for
tableaux below a Garnir tableau; and the four terminal alternatives for a
horizontal or vertical consecutive pair, the last alternative being $t^\mu$
for a horizontal pair and the corresponding Garnir tableau for a vertical
pair. No choice.

derivations.claim: **Counting addable and removable nodes (1).** Deleting the removable node $A$ of residue $i$ makes $A$ addable. Apart from this change, all corner changes occur immediately next to $A$ and have residues $i-1$ or $i+1$, which differ from $i$ since $e\ge2$ (for $e=2$ the two neighbor residues coincide with each other). Hence the signed count of $i$-nodes strictly above $A$ is unchanged, as is the signed count strictly below it. There is no other addable or removable $i$-node in the row of $A$. Splitting the signed corner count of $\mu$ into its above and below parts and the removable node $A$ therefore gives $d_A(\mu)+d^A(\mu^A)=d_i(\mu)+1$.

**The Cartan formula (2).** Write $u_j$ for the basis vector indexed by $j\in\mathbb Z/e\mathbb Z$ in the free abelian group on residues, and choose $R$ greater than the number of nonzero rows of $\mu$. Put $b_r=\mu_r-r$. The signed corner vector is $\sum_i d_i(\mu)u_i=u_{-R}+\sum_{r=1}^R(u_{b_r+1}-u_{b_r})$: adjacent row-boundary terms cancel precisely when the corresponding node is not a corner, and the tail term cancels the artificial bottom boundary. For the empty partition this telescopes to $u_0$, so $d_i(\varnothing)=\delta_{i,0}=(\Lambda_0,\alpha_i)$. Adding a node of residue $j$ moves one $b_r=j-1$ to $j$ and changes this vector by $u_{j+1}-2u_j+u_{j-1}$. Thus each $d_i$ changes by $-a_{ij}$, including the double neighbor contribution when $e=2$. The vector with coordinates $(\Lambda_0-\alpha,\alpha_i)$ has the same initial value and the same change when $\alpha$ increases by $\alpha_j$. Induction on the number of nodes proves (2).

**Bricks in the first row (5)(i).** All nodes carrying $m,\ldots,d$ lie consecutively in one row, by [F4] and standardness; since they are the largest entries, they form the rightmost segment of that row. At every addition in the codegree recursion for a brick in row one, there are no rows strictly above, so the increment is zero. Summing these increments proves $\operatorname{codeg}(T)=\operatorname{codeg}(T_{\le m-1})$.

**The defect recursion (3).** Expanding, $\operatorname{def}(\alpha)-\operatorname{def}(\alpha-\alpha_i)=(\Lambda_0,\alpha_i)-((\alpha,\alpha)-(\alpha-\alpha_i,\alpha-\alpha_i))/2=(\Lambda_0,\alpha_i)-(\alpha,\alpha_i)+(\alpha_i,\alpha_i)/2=d_i(\mu)+1$ by (2) and $(\alpha_i,\alpha_i)=2$, which is the displayed recursion [F3].

**Degree plus codegree (4).** For $d=0$ both definitions give $0=\operatorname{def}(0)$. For $d>0$ let $A$ be the node containing $d$ and $i=\operatorname{res}A$; by the induction hypothesis applied to $T_{\le d-1}$ and by step 2.1, $\deg(T)+\operatorname{codeg}(T)=\deg(T_{\le d-1})+\operatorname{codeg}(T_{\le d-1})+d_A(\mu)+d^A(\mu^A)=\operatorname{def}(\alpha-\alpha_i)+d_i(\mu)+1=\operatorname{def}(\alpha)$, where the middle equality uses (1) [F2, F3].

**Full residue bricks (5)(ii).** Suppose the terminal brick has $e$ nodes in row $r$ and occupies columns $c+1,\ldots,c+e$. Put $\lambda=T_{\le m-1}$. If $r=1$, step 1.3 applies. If $r>1$, standardness implies that all nodes in rows above $r$ already occur in $\lambda$ and that $\lambda_{r-1}\ge c+e$: each entry above a brick node is smaller, and all entries outside the terminal brick are at most $m-1$. Immediately before each of the $e$ additions, row $r$ therefore has length strictly smaller than $\lambda_{r-1}$. The signed corner counts strictly above row $r$ stay fixed throughout these pre-addition shapes. Indeed, in the top $r-1$ rows each maximal plateau of equal row lengths contributes one addable node at the start of its first row and one removable node at the end of its last row, and the last such row remains removable because its length is greater than that of row $r$ before the addition. Thus the number of addable corners above the brick equals the number of removable corners above it. The brick residues $(c+1-r),\ldots,(c+e-r)$ run through $I$ once. Summing the codegree increment for these residues counts each of the fixed above addable corners once positively and each above removable corner once negatively, giving zero. Hence the codegrees before and after the brick agree. The boundary count, defect recursion and tableau induction establish all five clauses by finite computations and use no choice.

([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) that is free as an $R$-module on a
finite set $C=\{c^{\lambda}_{st}:\lambda\in\Lambda,\ s,t\in T(\lambda)\}$,
where $(\Lambda,\unrhd)$ is a finite poset ([[def-partial-order]]; its strict
order is written $\rhd$) and each $T(\lambda)$ is a finite set. For
$\lambda\in\Lambda$ let $A^{\rhd\lambda}$ be the $R$-submodule of $A$ spanned
by all $c^{\mu}_{uv}$ with $\mu\rhd\lambda$.

Then $(C,\Lambda)$ is a **cellular basis** of $A$, and $A$ is a **cellular
algebra**, if:

(i) the $R$-linear map $i:A\to A$ with $i(c^{\lambda}_{st})=c^{\lambda}_{ts}$
for all $\lambda,s,t$ is an algebra anti-automorphism of $A$, i.e. $i(ab)=i(b)i(a)$
and $i(1)=1$ (equivalently $i$ is an isomorphism of $A$ with the opposite
algebra; the displayed formula forces $i^2=\mathrm{id}$); and

(ii) for every $\lambda\in\Lambda$, every $t\in T(\lambda)$ and every $a\in A$
there exist $r_v\in R$ ($v\in T(\lambda)$) with
$$c^{\lambda}_{st}\,a\equiv\sum_{v\in T(\lambda)}r_v\,c^{\lambda}_{sv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}.$$

**Cell modules.** For $\lambda\in\Lambda$ let $C^{\lambda}$ be the free
$R$-module with basis $\{c^{\lambda}_t:=c^{\lambda}_{tt}:t\in T(\lambda)\}$;
condition (ii) makes $C^{\lambda}$ a right $A$-module by
$c^{\lambda}_t a:=\sum_v r_vc^{\lambda}_v$ when
$c^{\lambda}_{tt}a\equiv\sum_v r_vc^{\lambda}_{tv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}$, and
it makes $C^{\lambda}$ a left $A$-module via $i$, the left action being
$a\cdot c^{\lambda}_t:=c^{\lambda}_t\,i(a)$. Both actions are well defined on
the freely spanning basis elements by (ii): the coefficients $r_v$ are unique
because $C$ is an $R$-basis of $A$ and the quotient by $A^{\rhd\lambda}$ kills
exactly the basis elements indexed by strictly larger labels, while applying
the anti-automorphism (i) to (ii) gives the same triangularity for left
multiplication. The module $C^{\lambda}$ is the **(right) cell module** of
$\lambda$, and
$$A^{\unrhd\lambda}/A^{\rhd\lambda}\cong C^{\lambda}\otimes_R C^{\lambda}$$
via $c^{\lambda}_{st}+A^{\rhd\lambda}\mapsto c^{\lambda}_s\otimes c^{\lambda}_t$,
where $A^{\unrhd\lambda}$ is spanned by all $c^{\mu}_{uv}$ with
$\mu\unrhd\lambda$. A cellular algebra may have several cellular bases.

Let $e\in\{2,3,4,\dots\}\cup\{\infty\}$ and let $\lambda\vdash n$ be a partition
with parts $\lambda_1\ge\lambda_2\ge\cdots$ and conjugate $\lambda'$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). Then $\lambda$ is
**$e$-regular** when every positive integer occurs as a part of $\lambda$ fewer
than $e$ times, i.e. $z_j(\lambda)<e$ for every $j\ge1$, and **$e$-restricted**
when $\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}<e$ for every $i\ge1$ (with $\lambda_i:=0$ for
$i>\ell(\lambda)$).

For finite $e$ these are exactly the $p$-regular and $p$-restricted notions of
[[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]] with $p=e$. For $e=\infty$ both
conditions are vacuous, so every partition is both $e$-regular and
$e$-restricted: the inequalities $z_j(\lambda)<\infty$ and
$\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}<\infty$ hold because partitions have finitely many
nonzero parts and each difference is a nonnegative integer. Moreover $\lambda$
is $e$-restricted if and only if its conjugate $\lambda'$ is $e$-regular: the
multiplicity of the part $i$ in $\lambda'$ is the number of columns of
$[\lambda]$ of height exactly $i$, namely $\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}$, so the
two conditions $z_i(\lambda')=\lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}<e$ are the same family
of inequalities, and for $e=\infty$ both sides hold. In particular
$\varnothing$ is simultaneously $e$-regular and $e$-restricted for every $e$
([[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]]).

Let $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ be partitions of the same integer $n$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). We say that
$\lambda$ **dominates** $\mu$, and write $\lambda\unrhd\mu$, exactly when
$$\sum_{i=1}^{r}\lambda_i\;\ge\;\sum_{i=1}^{r}\mu_i\qquad\text{for every }r\ge1,$$
where each sequence is padded with zeros beyond its number of parts; since both
partitions have total $n$, both sides equal $n$ for all $r$ at least the number
of parts of either, so the condition is a finite family of inequalities between
integers. We write $\lambda\rhd\mu$ when $\lambda\unrhd\mu$ and
$\lambda\ne\mu$. The relation $\unrhd$ is the **dominance order** on the
partitions of $n$; we call $\lambda$ and $\mu$ **incomparable** when neither
$\lambda\unrhd\mu$ nor $\mu\unrhd\lambda$ holds.

Because it is defined by a family of non-strict inequalities between integers,
$\unrhd$ is reflexive and transitive. It is also antisymmetric: if
$\lambda\unrhd\mu$ and $\mu\unrhd\lambda$, then the prefix sums of $\lambda$ and
of $\mu$ are equal for every $r\ge1$, and subtracting consecutive prefix sums
gives $\lambda_i=\mu_i$ for every $i$ (both sequences are eventually zero).
Hence $\unrhd$ is a partial order on the set of partitions of $n$. For $n\ge1$,
the partition $(n)$ is its unique maximum and the partition $(1^n)$ its unique
minimum: for every $\mu\vdash n$ and every $r\ge1$ one has
$$\min(r,n)=\sum_{i\le r}(1^n)_i\;\le\;\sum_{i\le r}\mu_i\;\le\;n=\sum_{i\le r}(n)_i .$$

For $n=0$ the order is the trivial order on the one-element set
$\{\varnothing\}$.
